c1_let.title: Values don't change unless you say so
c1_let.text: let gives a value a name, and that's that. let mut is a public announcement that you might change your mind later. In Rust, you have to announce it.

c1_types.title: Every value has a type
c1_types.text: i32 is a whole number. &str is a bit of text. Write the type after a colon and Rust holds you to it. Names in braces get filled in.

c2_fn.title: Functions
c2_fn.text: fn makes a function. Its parameters each have a type, and -> says what it hands back. The last line, with no semicolon, is the answer.

c2_semicolon.title: The semicolon swallows it
c2_semicolon.text: Put a semicolon on the last line and it's a statement, not an answer. Now the function hands back nothing, which is not an i32. Rustc tells you to remove the semicolon. Listen to it.

c3_move.title: Giving it away
code: let gift = wine; // the wine moves
c3_move.text: A String has one owner. let gift = wine; doesn't copy it, it hands it over. After that wine is empty-handed, and using it is error E0382.

c3_clone.title: Buy your own
c3_clone.text: clone() makes a second one. Two bottles, two owners, nobody goes without. It costs a little more. Manners usually do.

c4_borrow.title: Borrowing
c4_borrow.text: & lends a value without handing it over. The function gets to look. When it's done, the owner still has it. That's what borrowing means, Barry.

c4_mut.title: Borrowing to change
c4_mut.text: &mut lends a value so the borrower may change it. The owner has to be let mut and has to say &mut when lending. Everybody agrees, in writing.

c5_one.title: One hand on the tray
code: let b = &mut tray; // fine: a is done
c5_one.text: One &mut borrow at a time, or any number of & borrows, never both. A borrow ends at its last use, so finish with one before the next one starts.

c5_look.title: No clearing while someone's looking
c5_look.text: last is still looking at the tray when clear() wants to change it: error E0502. Move the println! up, and the looking is over before the clearing starts.

c6_struct.title: Structs
code: struct Golfer { name: String, strokes: i32 }
c6_struct.text: A struct bundles named fields into one thing. Make one by filling in every field. Read a field with a dot.

c6_impl.title: Methods
c6_impl.text: impl gives a struct methods. &self means the method only looks. &mut self means it changes things, so the struct has to be let mut.

c7_enum.title: Enums and match
c7_enum.text: An enum lists the only values there can be. match picks an arm for each, and it must cover them all, or it's error E0004. _ covers whatever's left.

c7_option.title: Was that a yes?
c7_option.text: Rust has no null. A value that might not be there is an Option: Some(value) or None. To get the value out, you have to say what happens if it's None.

c8_result.title: Result
c8_result.text: Result is for things that can fail: Ok(value) or Err(reason). Like Option, you have to deal with both.

c8_q.title: Passing the blame
code: let r = find()?; // Err: return it now
c8_q.text: ? after a Result means: if it's an Err, stop and hand it to whoever called me. It only works in a function that returns a Result itself.

c9_vec.title: Vec
c9_vec.text: A Vec is a list that can grow. push adds to the end, len counts, and {:?} prints the lot.

c9_for.title: Looping without taking
c9_for.text: for f in friends hands each item to the loop and uses the Vec up. for f in &friends borrows each one instead, and the Vec is still there afterwards.

c10_lt.title: Lifetimes
code: fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
if a.len() > b.len() { a } else { b }
c10_lt.text: 'a is a lifetime: a name for how long a borrow lasts. Here the answer lives as long as both inputs do. Rustc asks for one when a function hands back a borrow and can't tell where from.

c10_scope.title: Borrows can't outlive the owner
c10_scope.text: spare is dropped at the closing brace, so a borrow of it can't be used after that: E0597, doesn't live long enough. Own the thing instead: move it or clone it.
